newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Rwanda calls for Belgian help to end crisis.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda calls for Belgian help to end crisis.

text.p: Rwanda on Wednesday urged former colonial power Belgium to take the lead in trying to end the crisis in the Great Lakes area of central Africa.

As the country's Tutsi-led government edged closer to all-out conflict with Zaire, Rwandan Ambassador Manzi Bakuramatusa appealed for the international community not to treat the crisis simply as a humanitarian problem.
"Belgium must take the lead... present events are the consequences of the past," he told a press conference.

Belgian Foreign Minister Eric Derycke said the country would host an international conference on the crisis and try and act as the 'motor' in efforts to draw up a solution, but ruled out the dispatch of any troops to the region.
"Under no circumstances," he told Reuters television.
"Belgium has shown (military) solidarity in Somalia, in Cambodia, in Haiti and in the former Yugoslavia. It is now up to others to take the responsibility in Central Africa," Derycke said.
Zaire, where hundreds of thousands of refugees are fleeing factional fighting, is a former Belgian colony and neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi are former Belgian protectorates.

When Rwanda exploded into violence in 1994, 10 Belgian paratroopers were slaughtered by extremist Hutu militias who went on to launch a genocide in which some one million people, mainly Tutsis, were killed.
Rwandan and Zairean troops traded mortar and machinegun fire across their common border on Tuesday night and Wednesday morning.
Kigali claims several leaders of the Hutu-insprired genocide of 1994 are hiding in refugee camps on the border, using them as a rearbase for counter-insurgency against Rwanda and Burundi.
Zaire accuses Rwanda of using Banyamulenge rebels as stalking horses to carve out a Tutsi-state in the region.

Bakuramutsa said inaction by the international community was about to allow another genocide to take place, but strongly rejected suggestions Rwanda was fighting alongside Banyamulenge Tutsis against army troops in eastern Zaire.
"Rwanda has not the military means to protect the Banyamulenge Tutsis," he said.
He said the crisis which had created hundreds of thousands of refugees was a problem for all humanity.
Derycke said that military solidarity would best be shown by countries which have no concerns related to their past, a reference to Belgian colonisation in the region.
He made his comments after discussing the crisis in Zaire with the Belgian Senate Foreign Affairs Committee.
Several senators accused the Belgian government of insufficient action and said that holding meetings and dispatching special envoys was not an adequate response.
Derycke will travel to Addis Ababa next week to discuss the crisis with representatives from the Organisation for African Unity.
